description: New EN/C1 independent Reading questions; unapproved teacher review draft.

tabs.title: Interpreting the Argument
tabs.description: Identify the implications of the author's claims.

tabs.title: Claims and Qualifications
tabs.description: Examine the structure and limits of reasoning.

tabs.title: Critical Application
tabs.description: Apply the argument to unfamiliar educational situations.

questions.q: In what sense is the author's position on educational improvement deliberately qualified?
choices: It regards perseverance as ineffective whenever pupils lack resources
It considers effort valuable but questions expectations that ignore conditions
It proposes eliminating grades to protect the enjoyment of learning
It assumes that personal discipline generally determines achievement
questions.explanation: The first paragraph recognises the value of growth while questioning improvement as a universal personal duty.

questions.q: What makes the contrast between the two pupils ethically significant?
choices: Their equally poor scores suggest different levels of natural ability
The first pupil has been given a less demanding assessment
The second pupil is necessarily using less effective strategies
Unequal access to help may be confused with strength of character
questions.explanation: The writer warns against treating access to resources as evidence of personal merit.

questions.q: Which development best illustrates the danger of treating every activity as self-improvement?
choices: A leisure interest begins to feel like another task that must produce results
Learners refuse to study anything that has no immediate practical use
School assessment becomes impossible without numerical grades
Students become unwilling to discuss ideas with other people
questions.explanation: The author cautions that turning leisure into optimisation can make curiosity an obligation.

questions.q: What does the author explicitly allow about the pupils' study habits?
choices: Neither pupil could improve without a change in home circumstances
Only the pupil with greater support can benefit from practical advice
Both may benefit from better strategies, although that is not the whole problem
Both should be given identical guidance to ensure consistency
questions.explanation: Better study strategies may help both pupils, but cannot create time or a quiet room.

questions.q: Why does the last paragraph retain the idea of individual responsibility?
choices: The proposed measures are intended to replace teachers' advice
A learner's choices matter only after all inequality is eliminated
Institutions should remove all consequences from students' decisions
Providing support should enable meaningful choices, not eliminate them
questions.explanation: The writer argues that institutional action makes personal choice more meaningful.

questions.q: How are the slogans about never giving up used rhetorically?
choices: As examples of advice that is sound even without practical guidance
As attractive encouragement that may feel like blame without support
As evidence that students prefer praise to constructive feedback
As explanations for why schools have stopped measuring progress
questions.explanation: The author describes the appeal of slogans but warns that they can shift blame to the learner.

questions.q: A school wants to help pupils who cannot study quietly at home. Which policy best fits the article?
choices: Give every pupil the same motivational poster
Replace homework with a single timed examination
Provide supervised study space alongside specific feedback
Make each pupil prove they have studied for an extra hour
questions.explanation: The conclusion proposes concrete practical support, including supervised study space.

questions.q: A pupil enjoys a novel without working towards a measurable target. How might the writer judge this?
choices: The experience can be valuable even without a charted outcome
It is only valuable if the pupil later achieves a higher grade
It prevents the pupil from developing a productive study habit
The novel should be replaced with a more measurable activity
questions.explanation: The third paragraph defends learning activities without measurable outcomes.

questions.q: What is missing when equally poor results lead to identical advice for pupils with different resources?
choices: Evidence that the pupils spent exactly the same time revising
Attention to circumstances that make effort more or less effective
A rule requiring pupils to improve scores at the same rate
A formal distinction between grades and other types of learning
questions.explanation: The second paragraph argues that the conditions under which effort occurs matter.

questions.q: Which school decision combines the writer's principal recommendations?
choices: Use progress charts as the primary measure of every activity
Reward all perseverance independently of its circumstances
Leave access to resources entirely to families
Offer practical support, specific feedback and opportunities to revise
questions.explanation: The final paragraph recommends study space, feedback and revision while retaining personal agency.
